title: Five things worth knowing this week
intro: Phone-first health AI, multilingual small-business calls, a consolidating contact-centre market, models trained on human listening, and where code-switching evaluation breaks down.

stories.title: A health voice assistant built for landlines and basic phones
stories.summary: Google.org has granted Israeli health provider Clalit $2M over two years to build a “Digital Front Door” voice assistant. Its speech recognition is being tuned to local spoken dialects, and the service is designed to work over landlines and basic mobile phones with no data connection. Interactions are anonymised, and the assistant will be piloted before any national rollout. Clalit plans to open-source the architecture and its cultural-adaptation frameworks so other health systems can reuse them. The announcement gives no accuracy or satisfaction figures yet, so how well it serves dialect speakers and people without smartphones is still an open question.
stories.implication: Phone-first health assistants will need testing with real callers across dialects and phone types, not just lab accuracy scores.
stories.question: If the framework is open-sourced, will health systems that adopt it need independent evidence of how it works for their own patients?

stories.title: Spanish-speaking callers are routine, even for small US businesses
stories.summary: Upfirst, which sells an AI phone receptionist, analysed 677,562 calls to 2,967 of its small-business customers between January 2025 and August 2026. Spanish made up 13.4% of calls, and 90% of the 1,102 businesses that received at least 50 calls got at least one call in Spanish. In a separate survey, 29% of 262 owners said a language barrier had cost them a customer. Among 270 consumers, 80% wanted to be told when they were speaking to AI, and 70% were comfortable with AI answering basic questions. These are a vendor’s figures from its own customers, so they describe its users rather than the wider market.
stories.implication: Even routine small-business calls are multilingual, so voice agents need testing on how they handle callers in other languages and whether those callers trust them.
stories.question: Would small-business voice-AI vendors value evidence on how non-English-speaking callers actually experience their agents?

stories.title: Customer-service voice AI is consolidating fast
stories.summary: In one week, two large customer-service platforms moved to buy voice-AI specialists. Salesforce agreed on 2 November to acquire Cresta, at a reported price of about $2.7B. On 5 November, Five9 agreed to buy Level AI for about $325M in cash; Level AI reportedly handles more than a billion customer interactions a year. In the same week, voice-AI company SoundHound said it would cut about 27% of its staff. Our reading, which the companies did not state, is that buyers are paying for voice AI already running at scale in customer service, while companies without that footing are under pressure.
stories.implication: As voice AI moves inside a few large platforms, their customers may want independent evidence of how these systems perform with real callers.
stories.question: Which of the newly combined platforms might need outside evaluation of call quality across languages and accents?

stories.title: An audio model trained to agree with human listeners
stories.summary: Hume launched an Audio Decision API that answers questions about a recording directly from the audio, such as how many people are speaking or whether a caller sounds frustrated, and returns a probability for each answer. Hume says the model was trained on more than 10 million human judgments. In its initial evaluation, the model agreed with the average view of a human panel 70.7% of the time, compared with 56.5% for a single human rater. Hume also sells a separate API that supplies ratings from trained human raters. These are launch figures from the company itself, and one overall score can hide big differences between easy and hard questions.
stories.implication: Large pools of human listening judgments are becoming training data in their own right, and human panels remain the yardstick these models are measured against.
stories.question: Is there demand for human-panel judgments on calls in languages and accents these models rarely hear?

stories.title: Overall error rates hide where speech models fail on mixed Yoruba–English
stories.summary: Researchers tested 11 speech systems on 2,000 short recordings in which speakers mix English and Yoruba. The best had an overall word error rate of about 66%, but that number mostly reflects the English parts. On the Yoruba words themselves, every system that attempted a straight transcription got at least 96.6% wrong; most simply failed to produce Yoruba at all. Errors were near-total at the moment a speaker switched from English into Yoruba, against 40–53% when switching back. Two systems with almost identical overall scores differed significantly at those switch points. The study uses a single corpus with far more female than male recordings, so results may not carry over.
stories.implication: For languages often mixed with English, one overall accuracy score can make a model look usable while it is failing the local-language part entirely.
stories.question: Should the evaluations we design always report accuracy separately for the local-language parts of mixed speech?

title: Five things worth knowing this week
intro: Signals on real-world voice AI, language datasets and evaluation opportunities — with questions for the 60dB team.

stories.title: AI speech tools could help more women farmers be heard
stories.summary: IFPRI and Farm Radio International are using real farmer calls to improve African-language speech recognition. Their work highlights why models trained on clean, scripted audio often struggle with actual calls, especially when women face barriers to participating in advisory services. The practical challenge is not simply recognizing a language in principle, but understanding the way farmers speak under real conditions. This is an implementation insight rather than a confirmed buyer request.
stories.implication: Field recordings and testing with real users could be more valuable than another generic speech dataset.
stories.question: Could agricultural voice-AI providers be potential buyers for our research and evaluation capabilities?

stories.title: Voice agents are being tested on real banking and healthcare calls
stories.summary: Cekura’s benchmark uses 70 caller scenarios spanning banking and healthcare, across 12 ranked voice models. It tests accents, interruptions, noise and switching into Hindi or Spanish. Each scenario is repeated three times to check whether a model consistently manages the same conversation. The focus goes beyond whether speech is transcribed accurately: can the agent handle a difficult caller, maintain the context and complete a task? This is a useful example of how some providers are defining evaluation problems.
stories.implication: This suggests a possible offering around realistic test scenarios and local-language evaluation, rather than only data collection.
stories.question: Could we build comparable test calls in African languages?

stories.title: Text performance does not predict spoken conversation performance
stories.summary: Researchers behind Omnilingua-AudioMC compared six speech-language models using 354 conversations in ten languages. Models that appeared capable when processing transcripts could struggle with equivalent spoken exchanges, particularly when they needed to remember information from earlier turns. This matters for assistants that have to follow real conversations, not just a single spoken command. The findings make a case for testing multi-turn speech interaction as a distinct capability, rather than assuming text evaluations are enough.
stories.implication: Multi-turn, task-based conversations could be valuable evaluation material for teams building voice agents.
stories.question: Should our pilot include conversations where speakers correct or change earlier instructions?

stories.title: A Sheng mobile-money speech dataset is already on sale
stories.summary: Safi Data is offering natural Sheng and Swahili-English phone recordings focused on mobile money. Mozilla Data Collective lists a one-hour sample with 51 speakers, a planned 50-hour corpus and a listed dataset price of $10,500. This is a vendor listing, not evidence that anyone purchased it. Its focus overlaps with ideas discussed for the Kenya pilot, so it is important to compare the actual audio, metadata, license, speaker diversity and task coverage before claiming a gap in the market.
stories.implication: The Kenya pilot needs a specific differentiator — such as more varied task interactions, robust QA, demographic coverage or stronger evaluation use cases.
stories.question: What could our dataset offer that this one does not?

stories.title: Silencio is investing in endangered-language collection
stories.summary: Silencio described a field project in Indonesia to document Kodi, a language with limited written resources. Its stated plan is to collect 50 hours of consented, transcribed and translated speech through paid local contributors, with a non-commercial public release. It illustrates that speech-data organizations are actively developing community-based recruitment, permissioning and language-specific collection processes. However, it is a project announcement, not evidence of buyer demand or a commercial sale.
stories.implication: 60dB may be able to differentiate through its existing systems for field recruitment, contributor management, training and QA.
stories.question: Should we position 60dB more strongly around its fieldwork and contributor-management systems?
